newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque strike violence worsens, most shops close.
newsitem.headline: Basque strike violence worsens, most shops close.

text.p: Mounting tension in Spain's Basque country erupted into violence on Friday in San Sebastian where police twice clashed with supporters of a strike called by the political arm of separatist rebels ETA.
Gunshots rang out in the old quarter, where protesters had marched, as police in riot gear surrounded the cobblestoned section of the northern resort city. A police helicopter circled overhead.
Police had broken up an earlier march by strike organisers Herri Batasuna (HB), firing rubber bullets in the air and triggering a stampede of protesters.
Basque police, angered by a jury's acquittal on Thursday of a man charged with killing two officers, said they were braced for a long night of street violence.
"We are taking this seriously," one policeman wearing a ski mask told Reuters. "These guys have some real balls if they want to mess with us right now (after the acquittal)."
HB, which is protesting at the imprisonment of most of its leadership, said the strike had been a success in most sectors and would not have turned violent without police provocation.
"There were very few violent incidents and only in response to the police," HB spokesman Joseba Permach told Reuters. "We had car caravans, pamphlets and informative pickets."
Police complained, however, that the pickets visited shops and cafes "terrorising" the owners. Many small businesses that had made a brave attempt to open in the morning, were shut by mid-afternoon.
HB protesters pounded on windows and shouted for an end to repression as they marched through the streets earlier, overturning rubbish bins to make barricades and smashing shop windows.
There were sporadic incidents between strike organisers and police in other parts of the Basque region and Navarre, which is 25-percent Basque, and police detained nearly 100 people.

Trains and buses maintained regular service, escorted by police in most of the region, but there were some temporary interruptions due to road blocks and barricades on railway lines that were later cleared away.
Most schools were open, despite receiving bomb threats, and bigger businesses and factories operated normally, police said.
Spanish and Basque officials called the strike a "complete failure" saying it had been barely heeded, while HB said nearly 90 percent of the business and education sectors had joined.
"It's been a complete failure despite the fact that the call to strike was based on threats," a spokeswoman for the ruling conservatives in the Basque region said.
"The Basque society has behaved beautifully...showing a capacity to overcome the fear and blackmail of HB."
HB sent threatening letters to businesses, schools and workers this week urging them to observe the work stoppage.
ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) has killed some 800 people in its 29-year campaign for independence.
The strike exacerbated tension in the region, already running high because ETA had stepped up its deadly attacks this year, killing six people including a Supreme Court judge.
A court verdict on the eve of the strike that freed the alleged killer of two police under Spain's fledgling jury system added to the climate of confrontation in the troubled region.
